newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident urges HK not to stifle dissent.
newsitem.headline: China dissident urges HK not to stifle dissent.

text.p: Chinese dissident Bao Ge has sent a letter to the future leader of Hong Kong, Tung Chee-hwa, urging the new government not to suppress political protest after the British colony returns to Beijing rule.
Bao, who was released from a labour camp earlier in June after serving a three-year term, warned Tung of dire consequences for Hong Kong if he failed to protect fundamental liberties.

Bao was speaking to Reuters from eastern Zhejiang province's Ningbo city, where he said he had taken refuge after leaving his home in Shanghai on June 10 to avoid police harassment amid tighter security in the run-up to the Hong Kong handover at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday.
"In the letter, I advise the Hong Kong authorities not to suppress peaceful protests by individuals or groups around the time of the handover," Bao said.
"In addition, any suppression will attract the anger of the international community and may damage the reputation of both China and Hong Kong," he said, adding that the letter was mailed on June 25.

Tung, chosen by a Beijing-picked committee to become chief executive of Hong Kong after the British colony reverts to Chinese sovereignty, has said peaceful protests would be allowed except in cases advocating the independence of Taiwan or Tibet, or attacks on Beijing leaders.

Democratic activists in Hong Kong and around the world have expressed concern that Beijing will restrict personal and press freedoms in the territory despite pledging to preserve its freewheeling way of life for 50 years after the handover.
Under revisions to laws prepared by Hong Kong's new, Beijing-appointed legislature and due to come into force at midnight on Monday, police approval will be required to stage protests.
Protesters are now required only to notify police of their activities.

Tung has urged pro-democracy activists not to hold planned protests on the balcony of the building where Hong Kong's new Beijing-selected legislature will be sworn in shortly after the handover early on Tuesday morning.
Bao said he had planned no protests against the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule, which he supported, but had left Shanghai after threats from the police.
"I support the return of Hong Kong to Chinese rule," he said. "But the Public Security Bureau went to my house many times to threaten my family and the atmosphere was very tense."

Bao had been a member of the Shanghai-based Association for Human Rights, but was better known to the authorities as a campaigner for compensation from Tokyo for Chinese victims of Japanese war atrocities.
